title: Following the direction field
sub: How numerical methods follow a flow, and what a nonlinear flow can do.

frames.caption: The simple oscillator x″ = −x, plotted as position against velocity. The exact solution goes round the unit circle (grey) forever. Euler's method (orange) takes steps of h = 0.1 along the current tangent.
Each Euler step goes along the tangent, which always points slightly outside the circle. So every step gains a little energy, and the orbit spirals outward.

After two periods, Euler's orbit has radius 1.87 instead of 1: the numerical solution creates energy that the real system does not have. RK4 (blue) uses four slope evaluations per step, cancelling errors up to fourth order, and stays on the circle to within about 10⁻⁷. Halving h cuts Euler's error by about 2×, and RK4's by about 16× (2⁴ = 16).
The van der Pol oscillator, x″ − μ(1 − x²)x′ + x = 0 with μ = 1, in the phase plane. Start one trajectory near the origin (blue) and one far outside (orange).
Near the origin the damping is negative, so the small orbit spirals outward, gaining energy. Far out the damping is positive, so the large orbit loses energy and spirals in.

Both settle onto the same closed loop, with amplitude 2.01, whatever the starting point. That isolated, attracting orbit is a limit cycle, and linear systems cannot have one: in a linear system, scaling a solution gives another solution, so closed orbits come in whole families.
